meanings.note: A female speaker says آسفة (aasfe) when apologizing.

examples.trans: Sorry for being late.
I am very sorry.

meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.

examples.trans: I didn't hear the bell.
Come before the school closes.

meanings.note: Core Levantine verb for 'come': past إجيت / إجت, b-present باجي / بتيجي.

examples.trans: Why didn't you come yesterday?
Next time I'll come with you.

meanings.note: With contracted عـ + الـ, عالفيلم means 'to the movie'.

examples.trans: We watched a good movie yesterday.
What's the name of the new movie?

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'yesterday' (related to البارحة).

examples.trans: We watched the movie yesterday.
Where were you yesterday evening?

meanings.note: Past tense linking verb (كنت، كنتي، كان، كنا) and subjunctive تكون / نكون ('to be'); ما كان عندي means 'I didn't have'.

examples.trans: I was at school in the morning.
Today was very long.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'do' or 'make' (بعمل وظيفة 'doing homework', بعملوا مشاكل 'making trouble').

examples.trans: How did you do on the exam?
I didn't do anything wrong.

meanings.note: In Levantine school talk, وظيفة means 'homework' (كنت بعمل وظيفة) — a false friend if you only know its adult meaning 'job'!

examples.trans: We have math homework for tomorrow.
I finished the homework before bed.

meanings.note: Expresses location (عند باب الساحة), movement toward someone with لـ (لعندي 'up to me'), and possession (عندي وقت 'I have time', عنا 'we have').

examples.trans: I have class right now.
Come over to me for a moment.

meanings.note: Versatile noun: ما عندي وقت ('no time'), صار الوقت ('it's time'), وقتها ('at that moment / then'), مش وقته ('not the time for it').

examples.trans: I didn't have time to explain.
Everything is nice in its own time.

meanings.note: Warm or emphatic 'of course', used seriously or playfully between friends.

examples.trans: Of course I'll help you.
Of course I know the answer.

meanings.note: With كـ + الـ, كالعادة means 'as usual'.

examples.trans: Dina was late as usual.
I have a habit of reading before sleep.

meanings.note: Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.

examples.trans: Come here, Mariam.
Thank you very much, Miss.

meanings.note: Core Levantine question word for 'what?' (شو صار؟) and casual conversation starter ('So, ...').

examples.trans: What are you doing here?
So, ready to go?

meanings.note: Asks about manner or state (كيف كان الفيلم؟ 'how was the movie?', شفت كيف... 'I saw how...').

examples.trans: How are you today?
How did you get here?

meanings.note: Means 'go' (نروح 'we go'), and with على (راح علي إشي؟) forms the idiomatic Jordanian way to ask 'did I miss anything?'.

examples.trans: Come on, let's go to class.
I missed the bus this morning.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings: علي (on/about me), عليكي (to you, f.), عليها (to her), علينا (on/for us), عليكم (on you, pl.). Often contracts to عـ before الـ.

examples.trans: Count on me in this matter.
They lied about me in front of the teacher.

meanings.note: Signature Jordanian/Palestinian word corresponding to formal شيء; definite form الإشي, plural أشياء.

examples.trans: There is something important I want to say.
Nothing happened.

meanings.note: All-purpose positive adjective in Levantine Arabic for a good movie, nice weather, or sweet life (الحياة حلوة).

examples.trans: The movie was really good.
Our school is nice and big.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word (pronounced ktiir) used before or after adjectives ('very') and after plural nouns ('many').

examples.trans: The movie was really good.
I have lots of friends at school.

meanings.note: Derived from يا الله; urges action ('Come on, get off!') or wraps up warmly ('Alright, next time I'll come!').

examples.trans: Come on quickly, we'll be late!
Alright, we'll talk tomorrow.

meanings.note: Appears in المرة الجاي ('next time'), أول وآخر مرة ('first and last time'), بالمرة ('at all'), and plural مرات ('sometimes').

examples.trans: This is the first time I come here.
Sometimes we sit in the library.

meanings.note: Active participle of إجا; المرة الجاي (without feminine -ة in casual speech) is the standard Jordanian phrase for 'next time'.

examples.trans: I'll see you next week.
Next time I'll come with you.

meanings.note: Takes suffixes معي (with me), معك (with you), معها (with her), معنا (with us), معكم (with you all), معهم (with them), and forms مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!').

examples.trans: Come sit with us.
Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

meanings.note: Central setting: مدرسة الروابي للبنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls').

examples.trans: The school is close to our house.
I like going to school early.

meanings.note: With possessive -ي: مكاني ('my place / my spot').

examples.trans: School is my favorite place.
Stay standing in your spot.

meanings.note: Agrees in definiteness and gender with a possessed noun: مكاني المفضل ('my favorite place').

examples.trans: The courtyard is my favorite place at school.
This is my favorite song.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, كل means 'every' (كل يوم، كل إشي); with الـ (الكل) it means 'everyone'; with suffixes (كلنا، كلهم، كلها) 'all of us/them/it'.

examples.trans: Everyone knows the story.
We see each other every day.

meanings.note: In the past مع ما (ما عرفت شو أعمل), means 'I didn't know what to do'; b-present بعرف means 'I know'.

examples.trans: I know this place well.
I didn't know how to answer the question.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine demonstrative used before a definite noun (هاد الإشي، هاد الحكي) or as a pronoun (حتى لو هاد آخر إشي).

examples.trans: Is this book yours?
This isn't fair at all.

meanings.note: Marks topics (عني 'about me'), distance (ابعدي عن طريقي 'away from my path'), and defense (بيدافعوا عنها 'defend her').

examples.trans: We talked about the movie yesterday.
Stay away from her, please.

meanings.note: Plural صحبات is the everyday Jordanian word for girlfriends / school friends (صحباتي، صحباتها).

examples.trans: Dina is my closest friend.
I sat with my friends in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian/Levantine word for 'here' (formal هنا).

examples.trans: Come sit here next to me.
Life is very sweet here.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian pronoun corresponding to formal نحن.

examples.trans: We have been friends for a long time.
Come sit with us.

meanings.note: Takes a direct object or subjunctive verb without a linker (بنحب نقعد 'we love sitting').

examples.trans: We love sitting in the courtyard.
I loved the movie a lot.

meanings.note: In school speech, نقعد مع بعض means 'sit and hang out together'.

examples.trans: Come let's sit on the bench.
We hung out together at recess.

meanings.note: After مع, مع بعض means 'together / with one another'.

examples.trans: We walk home together.
We studied together yesterday.

meanings.note: Indefinite كل يوم means 'every day'; definite اليوم means 'today' (مش بعد اليوم 'not after today').

examples.trans: We see each other every day at school.
Today the weather is very pleasant.

meanings.note: With a possessive suffix, التاء المربوطة opens to ت: بحياتي ('in my life').

examples.trans: Life is sweet with friends.
I've never seen anything like that in my life.

meanings.note: Primary spoken verb for 'see' across the Levant, also used in farewells like أشوفك بكرة! ('See you tomorrow!') and نشوفك! ('See you!').

examples.trans: I saw everything with my own eyes.
See you tomorrow morning!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'tomorrow' (أشوفك بكرة! 'See you tomorrow!').

examples.trans: We have an exam tomorrow morning.
See you tomorrow at school!
